reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A deposition dermatosis with diffuse, non-pitting induration and thickening of the skin, typically over the upper back, posterior neck, and shoulders
The affected skin feels woody and firm, and movement of the neck and trunk can become restricted

Three recognised clinical settings: a post-infectious form after streptococcal or viral illness, an association with monoclonal gammopathy, and a form linked to long-standing diabetes (scleredema diabeticorum)
Unlike systemic sclerosis it spares the fingers and lacks Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and nailfold capillary changes
Histology shows thickened dermis with widely separated collagen bundles and accumulation of mucin (glycosaminoglycans)
The diabetes-associated form tends to be chronic and persistent, whereas the post-infectious form may resolve over months
There is no uniformly effective treatment; options explored include physiotherapy, phototherapy, and immunomodulatory approaches, alongside management of the underlying association
reference.pathophysiology: Scleredema is characterised by excessive deposition of collagen and mucopolysaccharide (mucin) in the reticular dermis, which thickens the skin and produces its firm, non-pitting induration. Fibroblasts in affected skin appear to be stimulated to overproduce collagen and glycosaminoglycans. The mechanisms differ by clinical context: a post-infectious immune response is implicated after streptococcal or viral illness, non-enzymatic glycosylation and altered collagen metabolism are thought relevant in diabetes, and a paraproteinaemic form is associated with monoclonal gammopathy, sometimes progressing to a plasma-cell dyscrasia. The dermal expansion, not oedema fluid, explains why the swelling does not pit.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing dermal thickening, separated collagen bundles, and mucin deposition
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for monoclonal gammopathy
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to assess for diabetes
Streptococcal and viral serology when a post-infectious form is suspected
Autoantibody screen to help exclude systemic sclerosis
redFlags: Detection of a monoclonal protein warranting haematological evaluation for myeloma or related dyscrasia
Restriction of chest wall movement or dysphagia from extensive induration
Rapidly progressive or widespread skin involvement
Features suggesting an alternative systemic sclerosing disease
reference.prognosis: The post-infectious form often improves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, whereas the diabetes-associated and paraproteinaemic forms tend to be chronic and refractory; overall prognosis depends on any underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing that the fingers are spared without Raynaud phenomenon
Failing to screen for a monoclonal gammopathy that may herald a plasma-cell disorder
Overlooking poorly controlled diabetes as the underlying association
Interpreting the non-pitting swelling as simple oedema
management: Treat the underlying association — optimise glycaemic control in scleredema diabeticorum, treat streptococcal or viral infection in the post-infectious form, and manage any monoclonal gammopathy
Recognise there is no reliably effective specific therapy, with phototherapy such as UVA1 or PUVA offering variable benefit for skin induration
Consider immunomodulatory approaches such as methotrexate, systemic corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin for progressive or disabling disease
In the paraproteinaemic form direct treatment at a clinically significant plasma-cell dyscrasia with haematology input
Provide physiotherapy to preserve neck and trunk mobility restricted by the woody induration
Distinguish from systemic sclerosis to avoid inappropriate treatment, given sparing of the fingers and absence of Raynaud phenomenon
Monitor the post-infectious form for spontaneous resolution and follow chronic diabetes- or paraprotein-associated disease long term
